- **BREAKING NEWS: EU leaders agree to amend the EU AI Act Just this morning, the EU announced it has reached a political agreement on the EU AI Act amendments. Although the law has not yet been formally amended, today's announcement is a clear signal that it is overwhelmingly likely to happen. There is a now a race against the clock to get the official regulation passed before the 2 August 2026 applicability date. Here are the key elements of the provisional agreement: ➡️ Delay of enforcement date for high-risk AI systems: from 2 August 2026 (in law today) to 2 December 2027 (for AI systems listed in Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (for AI systems covered by Annex I). These dates will be fixed, irrespective of the availability of standards and guidelines. ➡️ AI systems capable of generating non-consensual sexual and intimate content or CSAM added to the list of prohibited AI practices. ➡️ Registration in the EU's public database continues to be mandated for providers of "exempted" AI systems that are deemed to not be high-risk (due to a derogation)—but less information needs to be registered. ➡️ Postponement of enforcement date for generative AI output detection and watermarking obligation (stipulated in Article 50(2)) to 2 December 2026. ➡️ Broader scope for when organisations can lawfully process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction—but it must still be "strictly necessary" and only to address specific types of biases. Although the timeline changes are headline grabbing, the core structure and logic of the AI Act remains broadly intact. Organisations should not use the delays as a reason to deprioritise. In certain areas (e.g., registration), some of the initial Commission simplification proposals have been curtailed by the European Parliament and Council. Interestingly, no information was provided on what was agreed regarding AI literacy—the Commission and Council originally wanted to remove or significantly lighten the obligation, but the Parliament disagreed. Please note that this summary is based on the official reports from the EU institutions. It is non-exhaustive as the full text of the political agreement is not (yet) available. ...more ...more**

- **We've lived through decades of enterprise health software built for institutions. What comes next is patient-directed, patient-built, and sits on our side of the table. Not software. Not enterprise-ware. "Health me-ware". You heard it here first. Nick Dawson just launched OwnChart, the clearest example I've seen of what's next in health tech: patient-directed AI, built by patients, for patients. That phrase matters. Almost every AI tool in healthcare today is built for institutions and pointed at patients. OwnChart inverts the whole posture. Open source, self-hosted, patient-owned. You log into your patient portals the same way you would with MyChart, pull your full record into a place you actually control, layer in HealthKit data, photos, and scanned documents, then talk to any of it. Ask questions. Chase a hunch. Roll everything into a "dossier" around whatever you're navigating right now. For a couple of years now we've been pushing on Critical AI Health Literacy (CAIHL), the idea that the real unlock isn't access to AI, it's the active, examining stance patients take with it. Not the AI your hospital deployed at you. Not the AI a developer built for you. The AI you direct, on your own record, your own body, your own questions. - **Longevity medicine and cardiovascular prevention are converging. The tools are the same. The biology is the same. The gap is the framing. We have spent decades organizing cardiovascular care around events: the heart attack, the stroke, the decompensation that sends someone to the ER. That model made sense when the tools were limited to what you could do at the point of crisis. It no longer does. The shift toward integrated cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic care is one of the clearest signals that medicine has accepted this. Heart disease, kidney disease, and metabolic conditions are not separate problems sharing a patient. They are one problem expressed across organ systems. The cardiologist who treats the heart without tracking the metabolic trajectory, or without flagging the renal signal, is working with an incomplete map. AI diagnostic screening is the infrastructure that changes this. Not because the models are perfect, but because early, continuous signal detection creates a different kind of clinical opportunity than episodic measurement. The question is whether health systems are building around that opportunity or still organizing around the crisis. Every additional year we delay deploying the prevention infrastructure that already exists is a year of compounding cardiovascular events that were preventable. Longevity is not won or lost in the ICU. It is won or lost in the decisions made years before anyone ends up there.**
